items.prompt: Priya has never worked on mobile power management but is asked to weigh in on a background-sync change tonight. What is the actual trade-off she's facing?
choices: Whether to admit upfront that she lacks mobile expertise, or quietly approve the change and hope the risk doesn't surface
Whether this specific call needs her personal depth in mobile power management, or whether borrowed judgment from the right expert is enough
Whether mobile engineering is inherently harder to reason about than the domains she already knows well
Whether to postpone the decision until she can set aside real time to personally study mobile power management
items.explanation: The real choice isn't binary between faking it and refusing — it's deciding whether this decision genuinely requires Priya's own depth, or whether finding and questioning the actual domain owner produces a good enough call in the time available.
items.reference:
The claim: The breadth-depth trade-off is a decision about whether a specific call needs personal depth, not a choice between faking expertise and refusing to help.

Why: Priya can't become a mobile-power expert overnight, but she can find the person who already is one and ask a sharp question.

items.prompt: Why can't a staff-level role rely on personal depth in every domain it touches?
choices: Because depth fades in value once a person reaches a certain seniority and stops being worth building
Because the role spans far more domains than any one person can build real depth in, making breadth the only viable default for most decisions
Because showing deep expertise in a narrow area reads as a lack of trust in the rest of the team
Because domain experts generally resent being asked to help people outside their own team
items.explanation: The sheer number of domains a staff-level role touches — databases, mobile, infra, security, and more — makes personal depth everywhere mathematically impossible. Breadth has to be the default; depth is the exception earned by a specific call's stakes.
items.reference:
The claim: The breadth-depth trade-off is a decision about whether a specific call needs personal depth, not a choice between faking expertise and refusing to help.

Why: Priya can't become a mobile-power expert overnight, but she can find the person who already is one and ask a sharp question.

items.prompt: What does 'breadth' mean in this unit's framework?
choices: Never having to consult anyone else before making a call in an unfamiliar domain, no matter the stakes
Working familiarity with a domain — knowing it exists, roughly what it does, who owns it, and enough vocabulary to ask a sharp question — without doing the work yourself
Reading every available document about a topic thoroughly before acting on a decision that touches it
Being equally expert in every single domain a broad role happens to touch over a career
items.explanation: Breadth is deliberately lighter than depth: enough orientation to know who to ask and what to ask them, not the ability to personally verify or perform the work.
items.reference:
The claim: The breadth-depth trade-off is a decision about whether a specific call needs personal depth, not a choice between faking expertise and refusing to help.

Why: Priya can't become a mobile-power expert overnight, but she can find the person who already is one and ask a sharp question.

items.prompt: What do 'faking depth you don't have' and 'insisting on real depth for a low-stakes call' have in common as mistakes?
choices: Neither is actually a mistake — both are reasonable defaults depending on personal style
Both treat breadth-vs-depth as an accident of available time instead of a decision made deliberately based on the call's actual stakes
Both always take roughly the same amount of time to recover from once noticed
Both only happen to people who are still early in their careers and haven't learned better
items.explanation: They look like opposite errors — one under-investing, one over-investing — but both come from not deliberately sizing the response to the decision's actual stakes, reversibility, and how fast a wrong call would surface.
items.reference:
The claim: Faking depth and over-investing in unnecessary depth are the same underlying mistake: not deciding breadth-vs-depth on purpose.

Why: Both skip the deliberate sizing step and default to whatever's easiest or feels safest in the moment, rather than what the decision actually needs.

items.prompt: Someone spends three days learning the internals of a system before weighing in on a decision that was low-stakes, reversible in minutes, and would have surfaced any problem within the hour. What went wrong?
choices: Nothing — spending extra time to be thorough is always the safer choice to make
They over-invested in depth the decision's actual stakes didn't warrant, burning days a decision never needed
They should have faked expertise instead to save the three days entirely
The real mistake was not asking anyone else at all before starting their research
items.explanation: Depth has a real cost — time that could go elsewhere. Spending three days on a call that a twenty-minute conversation would have settled just as well is the over-investment failure mode, not a safer default.
items.reference:
The claim: Faking depth and over-investing in unnecessary depth are the same underlying mistake: not deciding breadth-vs-depth on purpose.

Why: Both skip the deliberate sizing step and default to whatever's easiest or feels safest in the moment, rather than what the decision actually needs.

items.prompt: What is 'borrowed judgment'?
choices: Copying a decision another team made earlier without checking whether it actually applies here
Making a decision based on a trusted expert's reasoning, while still sanity-checking what they said rather than accepting it blindly
Asking someone else to make the decision for you so you don't have to own the call
A polite synonym for guessing when no real expert happens to be available
items.explanation: Borrowed judgment is deliberately not blind trust — it means relying on someone else's real depth while still checking their reasoning, the way Priya asks Marcus how he knows canary rollouts actually catch drain issues instead of just accepting his answer.
items.reference:
The claim: Borrowed judgment means relying on an expert's reasoning while still sanity-checking it — not passive acceptance.

Why: Priya asks Marcus for his reasoning and track record before acting on his answer, rather than treating his verdict alone as sufficient.

items.prompt: Why does borrowed judgment still require sanity-checking the expert's answer, rather than just trusting it?
choices: Because experts are usually wrong, so every answer needs independent confirmation first
Because even a real expert's answer can be incomplete or mistaken, and accepting it uncritically defeats the purpose of exercising judgment at all
Because sanity-checking an expert's answer is required by most companies' written policies
Because asking a follow-up question takes about the same amount of time either way
items.explanation: The goal isn't finding someone to hand the decision to — it's making a better-informed call than guessing. Skipping the sanity-check turns borrowed judgment back into blind trust, which is a different (and riskier) thing.
items.reference:
The claim: Borrowed judgment means relying on an expert's reasoning while still sanity-checking it — not passive acceptance.

Why: Priya asks Marcus for his reasoning and track record before acting on his answer, rather than treating his verdict alone as sufficient.

items.prompt: In this unit's framework, what does 'stakes' measure?
choices: How senior the person making the decision happens to be in the organization
How much damage a wrong call in this specific decision actually does
How much time is available before the decision has to be made
How many people are watching or will notice the decision get made
items.explanation: Stakes is specifically about the magnitude of harm from being wrong — not seniority, urgency, or visibility, which are related but different things.
items.reference:
The claim: Stakes, reversibility, and time-to-signal are three separate factors, and a call needing depth is high on at least one of them.

Why: Priya's sync-interval call was high-stakes (millions of users) and slow-to-signal (drain surfaces over weeks), which is what pushed it toward needing real care rather than a quick skim.

items.prompt: A one-line copy change to an internal admin tool has low stakes, is reversible in seconds, and any problem would be noticed immediately. What does the framework suggest about this call?
choices: It needs the same careful depth as any high-risk decision, regardless of these three factors
Breadth is enough here — none of the three factors is high, so a quick check and a light question is right-sized
It should be escalated to the most senior available person regardless of the actual stakes
It cannot be safely decided without first consulting a dedicated domain expert
items.explanation: When stakes, reversibility, and time-to-signal are all low, insisting on real depth would be over-investment — the framework says breadth (a quick check, a light question) is the right-sized response.
items.reference:
The claim: Stakes, reversibility, and time-to-signal are three separate factors, and a call needing depth is high on at least one of them.

Why: Priya's sync-interval call was high-stakes (millions of users) and slow-to-signal (drain surfaces over weeks), which is what pushed it toward needing real care rather than a quick skim.

items.prompt: What does 'reversibility' measure in this framework?
choices: How popular the decision is with the team
How cheaply a wrong call can be undone once discovered
How long the decision took to make
Whether the decision was documented in writing
items.explanation: Reversibility is about undo cost — a feature flag flipped back in minutes is highly reversible; a shipped schema migration or public API contract is not.
items.reference:
The claim: Reversibility measures how cheaply a wrong call can be undone, independent of how damaging the call would be if never corrected.

Why: A client-side config flag is cheaply reversible; a shipped mobile release with a new sync interval is not undone as easily.

items.prompt: A change ships as a client-side config flag that can be flipped back within minutes if something goes wrong. How does this affect whether real depth is warranted, compared to an equally risky change shipped as a permanent schema migration?
choices: It has no effect at all — reversibility doesn't factor into the framework, only stakes does
High reversibility lowers the case for real depth, since a wrong call can be cheaply undone rather than causing lasting damage
It always eliminates any need for even a quick expert conversation
It automatically makes the decision low-stakes as well as reversible
items.explanation: Reversibility is one of three independent factors — high reversibility weakens the case for real depth even if stakes are otherwise significant, because a mistake can be cheaply corrected rather than locked in.
items.reference:
The claim: Reversibility measures how cheaply a wrong call can be undone, independent of how damaging the call would be if never corrected.

Why: A client-side config flag is cheaply reversible; a shipped mobile release with a new sync interval is not undone as easily.

items.prompt: What does 'time-to-signal' measure?
choices: How quickly a proposed decision gets formally approved by stakeholders
How fast a wrong call would surface on its own, before it causes real damage
How long a domain expert typically takes to respond to a question
How much time was spent researching a topic before the decision was made
items.explanation: Time-to-signal is about detection speed for a mistake — a crash surfaces in the next hour's dashboard; battery drain surfaces gradually over weeks of complaints.
items.reference:
The claim: A slow time-to-signal is dangerous because a wrong call keeps causing damage for a long stretch before anyone notices.

Why: Battery drain doesn't crash anything immediately — it shows up gradually in reviews and support tickets, well after the change has already shipped to everyone.

items.prompt: Why does a slow time-to-signal make a wrong call more dangerous than an equally bad call that fails fast?
choices: It doesn't — the speed at which a mistake is detected has no real bearing on danger
A slow signal lets a mistake keep causing damage, undetected, for far longer before anyone can respond to it
Slow signals are always the result of a team simply lacking good monitoring tools
Fast-failing mistakes are always more expensive to fix than slow-failing ones
items.explanation: A mistake that surfaces in the next hour's dashboard gets caught and stopped quickly; a mistake like battery drain, which shows up only gradually in reviews and support volume, keeps compounding for weeks before anyone even knows to look.
items.reference:
The claim: A slow time-to-signal is dangerous because a wrong call keeps causing damage for a long stretch before anyone notices.

Why: Battery drain doesn't crash anything immediately — it shows up gradually in reviews and support tickets, well after the change has already shipped to everyone.

items.prompt: According to the decision flow, does a call need real depth only when all three factors — stakes, reversibility, time-to-signal — are high?
choices: Yes, the flowchart requires all three factors to be high before real depth is warranted
No — being high on any one of the three is enough to warrant real depth, not all three at once
No, only stakes matters for this decision; the other two factors are irrelevant noise
Depth is only warranted when none of the three factors apply to the decision at all
items.explanation: The flowchart's condition is an OR, not an AND: high stakes, OR poor reversibility, OR slow time-to-signal is enough on its own to push a call toward needing real depth or careful borrowed judgment.
items.reference:
The claim: A call needs real depth if it's high on any one of stakes, poor reversibility, or slow time-to-signal — not only when all three are high at once.

Why: Priya's call was high-stakes and slow-to-signal but only medium on reversibility — two of three factors were enough to push it toward careful handling.

items.prompt: A decision is low-stakes and highly reversible, but a wrong call wouldn't surface for months. Does the framework say breadth is enough here?
choices: Yes, since two of the three factors — stakes and reversibility — are both already low
No — a slow time-to-signal alone is enough to warrant real care, even with low stakes and high reversibility
It depends entirely on how senior the person making the decision happens to be
The framework simply doesn't apply to decisions that are slow to signal at all
items.explanation: Since any single high factor is sufficient to warrant real depth or careful borrowed judgment, a slow time-to-signal by itself is enough reason for care, even when the other two factors look low.
items.reference:
The claim: A call needs real depth if it's high on any one of stakes, poor reversibility, or slow time-to-signal — not only when all three are high at once.

Why: Priya's call was high-stakes and slow-to-signal but only medium on reversibility — two of three factors were enough to push it toward careful handling.

items.prompt: Priya's sync-interval call rated high on stakes and slow on time-to-signal, but only medium on reversibility. What does the framework say about this call?
choices: It doesn't need real care, since reversibility wasn't rated fully high on its own
It warrants real care — two of the three factors already crossed the line, and only one is required
The framework can't produce a clear answer when ratings on the factors are mixed
Medium reversibility on its own always cancels out an otherwise high stakes rating

items.reference:

items.prompt: When breadth is enough and borrowed judgment is called for, why does it matter to find the actual owner of a mechanism rather than the nearest available senior person?
choices: It doesn't matter — any sufficiently senior person's answer carries the same practical weight
The nearest senior person may have organizational knowledge without firsthand depth in the specific mechanism, producing a plausible but unverified answer
Because written policy requires escalating questions only to the most senior person available
Because junior engineers are never a trustworthy source for this kind of question
items.explanation: Seniority and proximity aren't the same signal as depth in the specific mechanism at play — someone senior can answer confidently from memory or general knowledge without having personally verified the claim, which is a weaker basis than it appears.
items.reference:
The claim: The right expert is whoever has real depth in the specific mechanism, not the most senior or most reachable person.

Why: A specific, checkable question forces a specific, checkable answer — a vague question invites a vague, unverifiable one.

items.prompt: What is the risk of defaulting to 'whoever answers fastest on chat' when looking for a domain expert?
choices: There is no real risk — speed of response correlates closely enough with actual expertise
The fastest responder may not be the person with actual depth in the relevant mechanism, producing a fast but unreliable answer
Fast responders in a chat channel are almost always the most senior people on the team
Defaulting to the fastest responder guarantees the resulting answer will be dishonest
items.explanation: Availability and response speed say nothing about whether someone has real depth in the specific area a decision touches — optimizing for speed alone risks getting a fast, confident, but ungrounded answer.
items.reference:
The claim: The right expert is whoever has real depth in the specific mechanism, not the most senior or most reachable person.

Why: A specific, checkable question forces a specific, checkable answer — a vague question invites a vague, unverifiable one.

items.prompt: Why does 'is this safe?' tend to produce a weaker answer than 'if this job runs four times as often, does it hold a resource long enough to matter, and how would we know if it did?'
choices: Because longer, more detailed questions are always inherently better than short, blunt ones
Because the vague version doesn't specify what dimension of safety matters or give the expert anything specific to check, so the answer can't be checked either
Because experts generally prefer being asked several separate short questions at once, not one long one
There's no real difference between the two phrasings — both would get roughly the same quality of answer
items.explanation: A vague question invites a vague, unverifiable answer. A specific question that names a mechanism and asks how it could be detected gives the expert something concrete to reason about, and gives the asker something concrete to sanity-check afterward.
items.reference:
The claim: A sharp question names a specific mechanism and asks how a problem would be detected, forcing a specific, checkable answer.

Why: 'Any battery concerns?' got Priya a vague 'should be fine'; naming the actual mechanism (wakelocks, detection method) got her something she could verify.

items.prompt: What makes a question to a domain expert 'sharp' in the sense this unit uses?
choices: It uses enough technical jargon that the person asking sounds credible to the expert
It names a specific mechanism or scenario and asks something the expert can answer with a checkable, falsifiable claim
It is phrased so the expert can answer with a simple yes or no, nothing more
It is asked as quickly as possible so it doesn't take up much of the expert's time
items.explanation: Sharpness isn't about tone or jargon — it's about specificity that produces a checkable answer, the same specificity signal `weighing-credibility` looks for in a written source, applied here to a live conversation.
items.reference:
The claim: A sharp question names a specific mechanism and asks how a problem would be detected, forcing a specific, checkable answer.

Why: 'Any battery concerns?' got Priya a vague 'should be fine'; naming the actual mechanism (wakelocks, detection method) got her something she could verify.

Because borrowed judgment still requires sanity-checking the reasoning behind an answer, not just its confidence or specificity
Because company policy requires two independent confirmations before any decision ships
Because Marcus's answer seemed to contradict something Deja had said earlier

Why: Priya asks Marcus how he knows canary rollouts worked before, and he points to two real past incidents — that's what makes the answer load-bearing, not just confident-sounding.

items.prompt: What is the difference between borrowed judgment and simply doing whatever a domain expert says?

Borrowed judgment includes checking the expert's reasoning or track record before acting, rather than treating their verdict as automatically final
Borrowed judgment specifically means ignoring whatever the domain expert happens to say

items.prompt: Learning enough Android internals to personally verify the sync-interval change would take Priya about three weeks. What does the framework say about spending that time on a call that turns out to need only borrowed judgment?

items.prompt: Why does this unit treat 'go build real depth' as an exception that has to be earned, rather than the safer default choice?
choices: Because building real depth in a new area is never actually useful in practice
Because the time depth costs is real and finite, so defaulting to it for every decision would leave no time for anything a role actually needs to cover
Because domain experts generally dislike being asked to double-check their own work
Because real depth is treated as relevant only for decisions made early in a career
items.explanation: If depth were the safe default for every unfamiliar decision, the sheer number of domains a broad role touches would make the job undoable — the framework treats depth as something earned by a specific call's stakes, precisely because its cost is real.

Why: Priya's goal isn't zero uncertainty about Marcus's answer — it's an honest sense of how confident it should make her, the same target `calibration` sets for a person's own predictions.

items.explanation: Nothing in the framework depends on the domain being technical — the same deliberate sizing and expert-finding sequence applies to a legal or compliance call routed to someone without that specific expertise.
items.reference:
The claim: The sequence Priya followed generalizes across domains; only which factor dominates and who the real expert is changes each time.

Why: A database sharding decision or a security control follows the same read-stakes, find-owner, ask-sharp-question, sanity-check sequence — just with different specifics at each step.

items.prompt: Marcus says past canary rollouts caught drain issues before. Priya then asks him how he knows that. What specifically does his follow-up answer add that makes it more trustworthy than the first?
choices: Nothing at all — simply repeating the same reassurance a second time doesn't add any real new information
It points to two real, specific past incidents where 1%-rollout telemetry flagged a problem before full release, turning an assertion into a checkable track record
It mostly adds volume, since hearing two separate claims in a row sounds more convincing than hearing just one
It shifts responsibility for the eventual decision from Priya onto Marcus personally, should it go wrong
items.explanation: The value isn't repetition — it's specificity. Naming two real past incidents converts 'this has worked before' from an unverifiable assertion into a checkable track record, which is exactly the kind of evidence `weighing-credibility` treats as a stronger signal than confidence alone.
items.reference:
The claim: Asking for a track record, not just a verdict, is what turns 'sounds right' into something a borrower of judgment can actually stand behind.

Why: Marcus's answer became load-bearing only once he named two specific past incidents, not when he first stated the general claim.

items.prompt: If Marcus had responded to Priya's follow-up with 'I just have a good feeling about it, it's always worked out,' how should that change how much weight his overall answer carries?
choices: It shouldn't change anything, since he already named a specific mechanism earlier in the conversation
It should lower the weight given to the track-record claim specifically, since a good feeling isn't a checkable track record the way two named incidents would be
It should make Priya trust Marcus less about everything he's said, including the mechanism itself
It should have no effect at all, since Marcus remains the real owner of the scheduler
items.explanation: Sanity-checking is granular — a vague 'good feeling' response to the track-record question weakens confidence specifically in that claim, without necessarily undoing the separately verified, mechanism-level part of his answer.
items.reference:

Why: Marcus's answer became load-bearing only once he named two specific past incidents, not when he first stated the general claim.

items.prompt: The unit asks what would have changed if Marcus had turned out to be wrong and the canary shipped with battery complaints anyway. What's the actual answer it gives?
choices: It would mean that asking an expert, instead of doing her own self-study first, was the wrong approach from the very start

It wouldn't mean the approach was wrong — sanity-checked borrowed judgment paired with a fast-to-detect mitigation is still a better bet than blind approval or self-study she didn't have time for, even though it isn't a guarantee
It would mean Priya should have simply blocked the release outright instead of shipping it behind a canary at all
It would mean the three-factor framework itself is unreliable and shouldn't be used for decisions like this one
items.explanation: The unit is explicit that the framework produces a better-informed bet, not a guarantee. A wrong outcome despite a well-run process doesn't invalidate the process — it's exactly why the canary mitigation exists as a backstop in the first place.
items.reference:
The claim: Sanity-checked borrowed judgment is a better bet than the alternatives, even though it can't guarantee a correct outcome every time.

Why: The canary rollout exists precisely because even a well-verified expert answer isn't a guarantee — it's the mitigation that catches a wrong call cheaply if one still happens.

items.prompt: Why does the canary rollout matter even in the scenario where Marcus's answer turns out to be correct?
choices: It doesn't matter in that case at all — a canary rollout is only ever useful if the expert turns out to be wrong
It matters regardless, because it converts a slow, hard-to-detect failure mode into a fast, cheap one no matter how good the underlying answer was, which is the real lever available to Priya
It only matters for legal and compliance reasons that are unrelated to the actual technical risk here
It matters only because Deja happened to recommend using a canary as an option earlier in the conversation
items.explanation: The canary isn't a hedge against Marcus specifically being wrong — it's a structural fix for the slow time-to-signal that made this decision risky in the first place, valuable whether or not the borrowed judgment behind it turns out to be exactly right.
items.reference:

Why: The canary rollout exists precisely because even a well-verified expert answer isn't a guarantee — it's the mitigation that catches a wrong call cheaply if one still happens.

items.prompt: The unit also asks what would change if the sync-interval change had shipped as a client-side config flag, flippable within minutes, instead of a permanent release. What's the answer?
choices: Nothing at all would change — the same canary-and-expert-conversation process would still be strictly required either way

The stakes-and-reversibility math would shift enough that a quick ship-and-watch, with the flag ready to flip back, could be right-sized instead — possibly without needing an expert conversation at all
It would mean the change should always be blocked outright instead of being shipped behind a reversible flag
It would automatically make the change low-stakes as well as more reversible, collapsing both factors into one
items.explanation: Reversibility is one of the three independent factors — making a decision cheaply undoable weakens the case for extensive care even when stakes stay the same, which is exactly what the framework predicts and the unit confirms explicitly.
items.reference:
The claim: A change that's cheaply and quickly reversible needs less upfront scrutiny than the same change shipped in a way that's hard to undo.

Why: A config flag flippable in minutes changes the reversibility factor enough that a lighter-weight response could be right-sized, even with the same underlying stakes.

items.prompt: Why does making a change more reversible potentially reduce the need for an expert conversation at all, according to the three-factor framework?
choices: Because changes that are easy to reverse are never genuinely risky in any meaningful sense to begin with

Because if a wrong call can be cheaply and quickly undone, the case for careful upfront analysis (which the conversation exists to support) weakens, even though stakes and time-to-signal haven't changed
Because domain experts generally refuse outright to discuss changes that are already flagged as reversible
Because reversibility always outweighs the other two factors entirely, overriding stakes and time-to-signal completely
items.explanation: Since any one high factor is enough to warrant care, the inverse also holds directionally — improving reversibility removes one of the pressures pushing toward real depth or a careful borrowed-judgment exchange, potentially enough to make a lighter response reasonable.
